title: Study Abroad Report: University of Glasgow
paragraphs: For two months, March and April, I studied abroad at the University of Glasgow in Scotland. In March I did my clerkship mainly at Queen Elizabeth University Hospital (QEUH), a community hospital in Glasgow, and in April with family doctors (GPs) in various parts of Scotland, and I was given very valuable experiences.

Glasgow is the largest economic city in Scotland, in the north of the United Kingdom. In addition, cultural and artistic activities are also thriving, and it is a famous production area of whisky. The town is full of vitality, with an atmosphere firmly rooted in valuing both one's own culture and others' culture, and it was very easy to live in.

Medical students of the University of Glasgow do their clerkship at QEUH, a huge acute care hospital with more than 1,600 beds. The geriatrics department I went to in March was broadly divided into the emergency outpatient department and beds, ward beds in a ward of about 180 beds in total, and the general outpatient clinic. In addition to clerkships in these three divisions, I was also able to experience a clerkship at an outside rehabilitation hospital, accompanying home-visit care, and taking part in bedside teaching with local students. Gratefully, the doctors welcomed me warmly, saying "Tell us whatever you want to do, such as history taking and physical examination of patients!" I struggled with the new environment and the unfamiliar accented English, but I received feedback from the supervising doctors and was able to deepen my learning every day about what to focus on as I proceeded with examinations. Coming into contact with conditions I do not see in Japan, such as celiac disease and the after-effects of polio, was also a valuable experience. The doctors and staff at QEUH were all truly kind people, and I was able to spend a fulfilling clerkship period. One of the things I learned in the QEUH clerkship is the importance of understanding the patient's life background. During the outpatient clinic I even met a case in which the family at home could not agree, and although the patient had decision-making capacity, they could not receive the rehabilitation they wanted, and their ADL had declined rapidly. I realized that understanding, from the family and living environment in addition to the symptoms, what problems lie behind the chief complaint leads to appropriate care.

In April, with the cooperation of Dr. Alec Logan, a GP who accepts exchange students from all over the world, I did clerkships at six clinics across Scotland. Primary-care-based medicine is characteristic of the United Kingdom, and GPs (family doctors) play that role. Centering on Dr. Alec's GP practice, I visited hospitals with diverse backgrounds, such as a hospital tackling the drug addiction problem in an urban area, a general surgical hospital at the foot of a mountain, and a GP in an impoverished area on a former coal mine site in the countryside, mainly observing outpatient clinics and also taking histories and examining patients. "Seeing the patient as a whole person" in primary care was a phrase I often heard, but the GPs proceeded with the consultation by grasping the patient's family, work and mental state, making it easy for patients to confide their troubles, and I was impressed by that attitude. The doctor advised me that in primary care, "reassuring" the patient is also an important job, that I should not utter words that cause unnecessary anxiety even about trivial matters, and that I should acquire the knowledge and skills to be able to explain why the situation is one in which they can be reassured. It was a valuable clerkship period in which I could deepen my learning from a viewpoint different from the polyclinic at a Japanese university hospital. The breadth of the role of other healthcare professionals and the role GPs play in the community were also impressive. A GP's clinic is run jointly by several doctors, but besides the doctors there are also consulting rooms for nurses and pharmacists, and they too can prescribe drugs. A division of labor is advanced, such that for long-term follow-up with medication, as in diabetes and menopausal disorders, one sees a pharmacist, while at every lunch everyone gathered and, chatting, discussed how the morning's outpatient clinic had gone, and I could see them practicing as a team while making use of their specialties. The GPs were also extremely knowledgeable about the problems of local healthcare as well as each patient's situation, and every doctor taught me things such as that in this area life expectancy is so many years shorter and that the proportion of a certain disease is genetically high. In fact, the character of GPs differed greatly from area to area in order to deal with local problems, which was very interesting.

Being able to meet so many people I could not have met unless I had come to Glasgow was also a great gain of studying abroad. In Scotland there are many doctors who have come from other countries to work, so in the hospital clerkship I had opportunities to talk not only with local students but with students and doctors from various countries (Malta, Myanmar, Nigeria and others). They were interested in Japan's healthcare system and told me various things about medicine in their countries too. Dr. Alec, the GP, looked after me especially throughout the whole clerkship period, giving me opportunities to take part in lectures and history taking with local students, and taking me to a GP lecture event at the University of Glasgow and, on holidays, to the opera and concerts, which were valuable experiences I will never forget. Of course, I was also helped by the doctors and excellent students I met in the QEUH and GP clerkships, and I cannot thank them enough.

It was my first time living abroad for two months and I was nervous, but I experienced many new things and spent intense time. I feel that the fact that I gained the ability to act on my own, and that I came to think more seriously than before my study abroad about what kind of doctor I want to be, are the parts in which I grew in my own way through this study abroad. Finally, I would like to express my heartfelt thanks to the doctors of the International Collaboration Office, the doctors of QEUH, the GP doctors, and everyone who looked after me in Glasgow, who gave me this valuable opportunity.
